# Head-to-head against Tunix `peft_trainer_v2`

Added `tests/end_to_end/tpu/compare_tunix_trainer.py` and wrote the results up in
[`docs/reference/training_engine_tunix_parity.md`](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/blob/chengnuojin-trainer-fix/docs/reference/training_engine_tunix_parity.md), whose §9 carries the (7)-(9) A/B on both models.
It drives `MaxTextTrainingEngine` and `peft_trainer_v2.PeftTrainer` over the same model, the same `algo_core.grpo_loss_fn`, the same micro-batches and the same optax transformation, plus an independently computed sum-of-grads / sum-of-denoms reference gradient.

Qwen3-0.6B from `gs://maxtext-model-checkpoints/qwen3-0.6b/2025-10-27/scanned/0/items`, `fsdp=8`, batch 8, f32, `gradient_clipping_threshold=0.0` (MaxText clips in its update kernel and Tunix never clips; leaving it on would mask the normalization difference being measured).

**Numerics.** At GA=1 the two are equivalent — identical loss `-0.26746895909309387`, gradients within `rel_l2` **2.98e-4**, weight deltas agreeing to nine digits. With GA=4 and ragged micro-batches (denominators 64/16/40/8) they diverge:

| | exact reference | MaxText | Tunix v2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| accumulated denominator | 128.0 | **128.0** | **4.0** |
| gradient L2 | 40.1691955 | 40.1839846 | 52.7629719 |
| `rel_l2` vs. exact reference | — | **0.006206** | **0.887693** |

MaxText matches the exact gradient to the same ~6e-3 jit-vs-eager noise floor it hits at GA=1; Tunix lands on mean-of-means, per its own `# TODO(b/491970038): update denom for sequence packing.` in `_fwd_bwd_step`. Trainer-vs-trainer is `rel_l2` **0.676**. Worth noting the weight deltas still agree to four digits, because Adam normalizes per-element magnitude — the error is in gradient *direction* only, so it will not surface as a step-size anomaly. This is change (4) in this PR, measured against the external implementation.

## Trainer parity: `MaxTextTrainingEngine` vs tunix `PeftTrainer v2`

Reproduced from [`tests/end_to_end/tpu/perf_parity/README.md`](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/blob/chengnuojin-trainer-fix/tests/end_to_end/tpu/perf_parity/README.md) on this branch, which supersedes the
2026-08-31 performance and HBM numbers this section used to quote. Those, and the (7)-(9)
host-path A/B, remain in [`docs/reference/training_engine_tunix_parity.md`](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/blob/chengnuojin-trainer-fix/docs/reference/training_engine_tunix_parity.md).

Consolidated conclusions from two studies run on a v7-8 (Ironwood) host, 2026-09-02 and
2026-09-03. **Both trainers drive the same MaxText model in every arm**, so what varies is
the trainer, the mesh and the sharding mode — never the implementation of the network.

Two models, chosen because they stress opposite things:

| | `qwen3.5-35b-a3b` | `qwen3-0.6b` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kind | sparse MoE, 256 routed + 1 shared expert, 40 layers | dense, 28 layers |
| Step time | ~0.7–2.3 s — device-bound, host cost invisible | ~50–470 ms — host and collective cost visible |
| What it tests | mesh choice (TP vs EP), MoE kernels, GA capability | sharding mode, optimizer-state sharding, host overhead |
| Detailed report | [`RESULTS-qwen35-35b-ep-20260902.md`](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/blob/chengnuojin-trainer-fix/tests/end_to_end/tpu/perf_parity/RESULTS-qwen35-35b-ep-20260902.md), [`RESULTS-qwen35-35b-20260902.md`](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/blob/chengnuojin-trainer-fix/tests/end_to_end/tpu/perf_parity/RESULTS-qwen35-35b-20260902.md) | [`RESULTS-qwen3-0p6b-zero1-20260903.md`](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/blob/chengnuojin-trainer-fix/tests/end_to_end/tpu/perf_parity/RESULTS-qwen3-0p6b-zero1-20260903.md) |

Every command needed to reproduce every number is in **[Appendix A](#appendix-a-reproducing)**.

#### Conclusions

1. **On raw throughput the two trainers are at parity, and the gap is a fixed dispatch, not a
   scaling one.** On the 35b model they land within 0.5% of each other at every mesh
   (670.3 vs 666.6 ms at ep=8; 2313.8 vs 2303.1 at tp=2), both above 99% device utilization.
   `PeftTrainer`'s lead is its single fused `jit__train_step` against the engine's split
   `fwd_bwd` + `update` — a constant ~16 ms, which is 0.7% of a 2.3 s step and a third of a
   61 ms one.

2. **Under explicit sharding the engine wins decisively, and the win is the engine's, not the
   mesh mode's.** This is the largest trainer-attributable difference measured. Setting
   `shard_mode=explicit` on qwen3-0.6b at GA=8 makes the engine **1.50x faster** (371.7 →
   247.4 ms) and `PeftTrainer` **1.31x slower** (356.8 → 465.7 ms) — the same flag, the same
   mesh, opposite signs. Same-mesh, same-mode, GA=8: **247.4 ms against 465.7 ms, 1.88x.**
   Under Explicit axes the engine's cotangents come out `unreduced`, so the data-parallel
   all-reduce moves out of every micro-batch into `update()`; tunix's step has no such path
   and simply pays the collectives literally where GSPMD had been optimizing them.

3. **The decisive difference is capability, not speed: `PeftTrainer v2` cannot do gradient
   accumulation on the 35b model at the tunix revision MaxText pins.** GA=2, 4 and 8 each OOM
   with a byte-identical 161.94 G against 94.74 G available. The engine has no such wall and
   its per-micro-batch cost *improves* with depth. Tunix `44a35eeaf` fixes it with one line
   (`GradientAccumulator.reset()` using `v[...] * 0` instead of `jnp.zeros_like`, which loses
   sharding inside a traced function and materialises the full 129 G tree). **Recommend
   bumping `src/dependencies/extra_deps/post_train_github_deps.txt` past that commit.**

4. **Mesh choice dominates trainer choice by an order of magnitude.** Moving the 35b model
   from `fsdp=4 x tp=2` to `ep=8 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort` is worth **3.45x** on both
   trainers alike. Nothing trainer-side in this study is worth more than 1.9x. Tune the mesh
   before arguing about trainers.

5. **For memory on small models, FSDP beats Zero-1 and it is not close.** 2.04 G against
   8.70 G at qwen3-0.6b/GA=8. Zero-1 shards the two Adam moments; FSDP shards the parameters
   and gradients too, and at 0.6 B those are most of the residual. Zero-1's advantage is that
   it adds no collectives to forward and backward — not that it saves more bytes. The engine
   forbids combining them.

6. **Neither trainer currently offers both speed and memory.** At qwen3-0.6b/GA=8 the engine's
   explicit path is 1.36x faster than `PeftTrainer` on FSDP but uses 6.2x the HBM — 4.3x even
   with Zero-1 on top. That is the open gap this comparison leaves.

#### Environment

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Host | 8 x TPU7x (v7-8 Ironwood, 4 chips / 8 JAX devices), single process |
| JAX | 0.11.1 |
| Shape | micro-batch 8 x seq 1024, f32 compute and weights, `remat_policy=none` |
| Wall clock | 23 steps, median of the last 19, `--no-trace` |

### 1. `qwen3.5-35b-a3b` — MoE, mesh-bound

40 layers, 256 routed + 1 shared expert, emb 2048, 16 query / 2 KV heads, head_dim 256,
vocab 248320. Scanned. `optax.sgd(1e-5)`, constant schedule, no clipping.

`--tp 8` is illegal on this model: `_validate_kv_head_sharding` requires
`num_kv_heads % tp == 0` and there are 2 KV heads, so `fsdp=4 x tp=2` is the widest legal
tensor-parallel shape on 8 devices.

#### 1.1 Trainer vs trainer, same mesh

| Mesh | GA | Engine | `PeftTrainer v2` | Δ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ep=8` + ring + ragged | 1 | 670.3 ms | **666.6 ms** | Peft 0.55% |
| `ep=8` + ring + ragged | 8 | 5343.0 ms | **5278.0 ms** ¹ | Peft 1.2% |
| `fsdp=4 x tp=2` | 1 | 2313.8 ms | **2303.1 ms** | Peft 0.46% |
| `fsdp=4 x tp=2` | 8 | **18405.3 ms** | OOM ² | engine only |

¹ tunix `07dbe293` (head). OOM at the pinned `c4ec573` — see §1.3.
² OOM at the pinned revision; not run at head.

Device utilization is 99.2–99.8% on every row. At 2.3 s of device work per step every
host-side difference between the trainers hides; the 0.5% that remains is the engine's second
dispatch (`jit__update_kernel`, 16.0 ms at ep=8 and 16.46 ms at tp=2).

Per-execution device cost, ep=8, GA=1:

| Arm | Modules | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| engine | `jit_first_kernel` 648.9 + `jit__update_kernel` 16.0 | **664.9 ms** |
| `PeftTrainer v2` | `jit__train_step` 663.0 | **663.0 ms** |

#### 1.2 The mesh is worth 3.45x, and the two trainers track each other exactly

Every row `--scan --seq 1024 --ga 1 --no-trace`, median of 19 steps.

| Mesh and flags | Engine | `PeftTrainer v2` | vs tp=2 | vs row above |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--tp 2` (fsdp=4 x tp=2) | 2313.8 | 2303.1 | 1.00x | — |
| `--tp 2 --ep 4 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort` | 1726.9 | 1704.3 | 1.34x | — |
| `--ep 8` (no MoE flags) | 1063.8 | 1059.7 | **2.17x** | 2.17x |
| `--ep 8 --ragged-sort` | 1047.6 | 1043.4 | 2.21x | 1.02x |
| `--ep 8 --ring-of-experts` | 720.1 | 717.4 | 3.21x | 1.48x |
| `--ep 8 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort` | **670.3** | **666.6** | **3.45x** | 1.07x |

* **The mesh is the larger half.** A bare `ep=8` with no kernel flags is already 2.17x. TP
  splits a 2048-wide embedding and 2 KV heads and pays all-reduces for it; EP splits 256
  experts, which is what this model actually has a lot of.
* **Ragged sort is a multiplier on ring-of-experts, not independently useful.** 1.02x alone,
  1.07x on top of the ring. `layers/moe.py` selects the `ring_ragged_sort` kernels only under
  `use_ragged_sort and use_ring_of_experts`.
* **Splitting the mesh across both axes is the worst of both.** `--tp 2 --ep 4` with both
  flags on (1726.9 ms) is slower than a bare `--ep 8` with none (1063.8 ms).

Wall and device speedups agree to two decimals (3.45x / 3.47x), which is what says the gain is
work removed rather than overhead rearranged.

#### 1.3 Gradient accumulation: a capability difference

At `ep=8` + ring + ragged, median ms/step:

| GA | Engine | per micro | `PeftTrainer`, tunix `c4ec573` (pinned) | `PeftTrainer`, tunix `07dbe293` (head) | per micro |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 670.3 | 670.3 | 666.6 | 667.3 | 667.3 |
| 2 | 1338.8 | 669.4 | **OOM** | 1339.6 | 669.8 |
| 4 | 2672.3 | 668.1 | **OOM** | 2651.8 | 663.0 |
| 8 | 5343.0 | 667.9 | **OOM** | 5278.0 | **659.8** |

```
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Ran out of memory on HBM, the total memory
required for HLO temporaries (161.94G) exceeds available HBM (94.74G).
HLO module: jit__update_step.
```

The figure is **byte-identical at GA=2, 4 and 8**, which rules out the obvious reading that N
micro-batches are live at once. The allocation is parameter-shaped, not depth-shaped:
`PeftTrainer._is_single_microstep()` is true only at `gradient_accumulation_steps == 1`, and
only that path skips allocating the accumulator.

**The cause is one line, tested directly.** Reverting only tunix `44a35eeaf` on top of head —
leaving the other 208 commits in place — brings the failure back byte for byte. `reset()` runs
*inside* the traced `_update_step`, and there `jnp.zeros_like` does not carry its operand's
sharding, so XLA materialises the full unsharded tree:

```
129.12 G  full parameter tree, unsharded, from the traced zeros_like
+ 16.14 G  the sharded accumulator itself
+ 16.14 G  one more sharded parameter-tree copy
= 161.40 G   measured: 161.41 G
```

Once fixed, the two trainers are at parity at every depth and `PeftTrainer` pulls 1.2% ahead
by GA=8, because it amortizes its update slightly better (667.3 → 659.8 per micro against the
engine's 670.3 → 667.9).

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

#### 2.2 Where the time goes

Per-execution device cost, `--steps 6` traces. A GA=8 step is one `first_kernel`, seven
`accum_kernel` and one `_update_kernel` on the engine; eight `_fwd_bwd_step` and one
`_update_step` on `PeftTrainer`.

| Arm, GA=8 | per micro-batch | update | Step total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| engine, auto | 43.57 ms | 5.95 | **354.19** |
| engine, explicit | **25.03 ms** | 27.81 | **226.19** |
| engine, explicit + Zero-1 | 25.07 ms | 30.71 | **229.51** |
| `PeftTrainer`, auto | 42.73 ms | 6.82 | **348.66** |
| `PeftTrainer`, explicit | 56.04 ms | 6.89 | **455.21** |
| `PeftTrainer`, fsdp=8 | 40.79 ms | 1.69 | **328.01** |

**The all-reduce is moved, not removed, and the same ~20 ms shows up three times.** Going
`auto` → `explicit` on the engine at GA=8: the first kernel drops 20.08 ms, each of seven
accumulates drops 18.54 ms, and the update rises 21.86 ms. That is one all-reduce of the 2.4 G
f32 gradient tree over 8 devices, which this host does in about 20 ms — paid eight times under
`auto`, once under `explicit`. Extrapolated from these kernels it is a 1.78 ms loss at GA=1
(measured at 4.63 ms in the GA=1 trace, which runs slower throughout) and **pays from GA=2 on**.

**`PeftTrainer` gets no such benefit; Explicit costs it 31%.** Its per-micro-batch step goes
42.73 → 56.04 ms while its update is unchanged (6.82 → 6.89). Nothing moves out of the
micro-batch — the collectives stay where they were and get more expensive, because Explicit
axes stop GSPMD from rearranging them.

**Zero-1 costs +2.9 ms, entirely in `update()`, and this is provable rather than inferred.**
The Zero-1 arm's `jit_first_kernel` and `jit_accum_kernel` carry *identical HLO program hashes*
to the explicit control's (`1445966014043162594` and `614701509375139023`), at both GA depths.
Only `jit__update_kernel` differs (`8707565451094719151`), by +2.90 ms at GA=8 and +2.85 ms at
GA=1 — the price of replacing the gradient all-reduce with a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather
of the updated parameters.

**FSDP does not supply a deferral either.** It cuts the per-micro cost only 42.73 → 40.79 ms:
sharding the parameters swaps the gradient all-reduce for a parameter all-gather plus a
gradient reduce-scatter, about the same traffic, still once per micro-batch. The engine's
explicit path runs the same micro-batch in 25.03 ms, **1.63x faster**, by not running the
collective there at all.

#### 2.3 Where the memory goes

At ~0.6 B params in f32: parameters 2.4 G, Adam `mu` + `nu` 4.8 G, gradients 2.4 G.

| | GA=1 | GA=8 | What is sharded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| engine, dp=8 auto | 9.95 G | 12.73 G | nothing — params, moments and grads all replicated |
| engine, + Zero-1 | 7.76 G | 8.70 G | the two moments, over `data` (4.8 G → 0.6 G) |
| *saving* | *2.20 G (22%)* | ***4.04 G (32%)*** | |
| `PeftTrainer`, fsdp=8 | 1.74 G | 2.04 G | params, grads **and** moments, over `fsdp` |

Zero-1's predicted saving is 4.8 − 0.6 = **4.2 G**; it delivers 4.04 G of that at GA=8 but only
2.20 G at GA=1, because with no accumulator live the high-water mark is set partly by the
activation peak instead. **Zero-1's saving is capped by whatever else is at the peak**, which
is why it looks better the deeper the accumulation goes.

FSDP's 2.04 G is not a better-tuned version of the same idea — it shards a strictly larger set
of tensors.

### 3. Which to use

| Situation | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Large MoE, GA=1 | either | Parity to 0.5%; pick on ergonomics. Spend the effort on `--ep 8 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort` instead — 3.45x. |
| Large MoE, GA>1, tunix at MaxText's pin | **engine** | `PeftTrainer` OOMs outright. Capability, not speed. |
| Large MoE, GA>1, tunix past `44a35eeaf` | either | Parity; `PeftTrainer` 1.2% ahead at GA=8. |
| Small dense, GA=1 | `PeftTrainer` | 46.4 ms on FSDP against the engine's 61.0. The engine's ~19 ms/step of host-side NNX graph work is a third of a step this size. |
| Small dense, GA≥2, throughput first | **engine + `--explicit`** | 247.4 ms against 337.4 (Peft/FSDP) and 465.7 (Peft/explicit). The deferred all-reduce is engine-only. |
| Small dense, memory first | `PeftTrainer` + FSDP | 2.04 G against Zero-1's 8.70 G. |
| Need optimizer-state sharding without FSDP | **engine + `--zero1`** | 1.3% for 32% of HBM at GA=8. Requires `--explicit`, which brings the deferral with it. |

Do not read the small-model host overhead as a general engine defect: on the 35b model the
same NNX graph work is 3.1 ms against a 714 ms step, 0.4%.

```bash
python xplane_device_summary.py --steps 3 <path>.xplane.pb   # per-module device time
python xplane_host_summary.py             <path>.xplane.pb   # host-side dispatch
```

---

### Appendix A: Reproducing

#### A.0 Prerequisites

A TPU VM with **8 devices** (these numbers are from a v7-8; other 8-device generations will
give different absolute times but the same comparisons). Then:

```bash
# 1. Fetch PR #5060.
git clone https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext.git && cd maxtext
git fetch origin pull/5060/head:pr5060 && git checkout pr5060

# 2. Install MaxText (see docs/install_maxtext.md) plus the post-training extras --
#    the PeftTrainer arms need tunix, which lives in the post-train extra deps.
install_tpu_post_train_extra_deps

# 3. Everything below runs from this directory. It matters: the arms import
#    perf_parity_common as a sibling module, and a working directory containing a
#    tunix/ checkout would shadow the installed package.
cd tests/end_to_end/tpu/perf_parity
```

The engine-side Zero-1 measured in §2 is **PR #5099**, not #5060. On a #5060-only checkout
every engine arm prints `zero1: UNSUPPORTED` or `zero1: DECLINED (...)` and the Zero-1 rows
become a second copy of the baseline — the runner greps for that line so it cannot pass
unnoticed. The other five arms of §2 and all of §1 reproduce on #5060 alone.

#### A.1 One command per study

```bash
./run_qwen3_0p6b_zero1.sh   [outdir]   # §2, six arms x GA{1,8}, ~20 min (~10 min --no-trace)
./run_qwen3_5_35b_a3b.sh    [outdir]   # §1, ~90 min
./run_qwen3_0p6b.sh         [outdir]   # the sgd/tp qwen3-0.6b shape, for reference
```

Each prints its step times, peak HBM and trace paths at the end, and writes one log per arm
into the output directory. They run serially — every arm wants the whole host, and two
concurrent runs will fight over the 8 devices.

#### A.2 Individual arms — §1, `qwen3.5-35b-a3b`

```bash
SHAPE="--model qwen3.5-35b-a3b --scan --seq 1024 --ga 1"

# 1.1 headline, both trainers at both meshes
python engine_profile.py       $SHAPE --ep 8 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort --no-trace
python peft_trainer_profile.py $SHAPE --ep 8 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort --no-trace
python engine_profile.py       $SHAPE --tp 2 --no-trace
python peft_trainer_profile.py $SHAPE --tp 2 --no-trace

# 1.2 mesh ablation
python engine_profile.py $SHAPE --tp 2 --ep 4 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort --no-trace
python engine_profile.py $SHAPE --ep 8 --no-trace
python engine_profile.py $SHAPE --ep 8 --ragged-sort --no-trace
python engine_profile.py $SHAPE --ep 8 --ring-of-experts --no-trace

# 1.3 gradient accumulation
for GA in 2 4 8; do
  python engine_profile.py       ${SHAPE/--ga 1/--ga $GA} --ep 8 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort --no-trace
  python peft_trainer_profile.py ${SHAPE/--ga 1/--ga $GA} --ep 8 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort --no-trace
done

# Device time.
PERF_PARITY_PROFILE_ROOT=/tmp/traces \
  python engine_profile.py $SHAPE --ep 8 --ring-of-experts --ragged-sort --steps 6
```

`--ring-of-experts` and `--ragged-sort` are rejected at `--ep 1`, mirroring MaxText, which
infers the EP rank from `logical_axis_rules` rather than from `ici_expert_parallelism` and
raises *"When EP rank is 1, use_ring_of_experts must be False"*.

The GA table's `PeftTrainer` head column needs tunix past `44a35eeaf`. Installing it without
touching the repo's pin:

```bash
pip install --no-deps "google-tunix @ https://github.com/google/tunix/archive/07dbe293.zip"
```

#### A.3 Individual arms — §2, `qwen3-0.6b`

```bash
SHAPE="--model qwen3-0.6b --seq 1024 --opt adamw"

for GA in 1 8; do
  python engine_profile.py       $SHAPE --dp 8            --no-trace --ga $GA  # auto
  python engine_profile.py       $SHAPE --dp 8 --explicit --no-trace --ga $GA  # explicit
  python engine_profile.py       $SHAPE --dp 8 --zero1    --no-trace --ga $GA  # + Zero-1
  python peft_trainer_profile.py $SHAPE --dp 8            --no-trace --ga $GA
  python peft_trainer_profile.py $SHAPE --dp 8 --explicit --no-trace --ga $GA
  python peft_trainer_profile.py $SHAPE --fsdp 8          --no-trace --ga $GA
done

# Device time. Trace the explicit control too -- shard_mode is not only a layout choice
# here, so the control compiles different kernels from the baseline.
PERF_PARITY_PROFILE_ROOT=/tmp/traces \
  python engine_profile.py $SHAPE --dp 8 --zero1 --steps 6 --ga 8
```

`--zero1` implies `--explicit`. `RunSpec` rejects the three combinations the engine would
reject anyway — Zero-1 with FSDP, with `data` of 1, and with `sgd` — rather than letting them
run and quietly measure the baseline.

#### A.4 Flags

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--model` | `qwen3-0.6b` | any MaxText `model_name`; only `qwen3_0p6b_tunix_profile.py` is model-locked |
| `--dp / --fsdp / --tp / --ep` | 1 / fills devices / 1 / 1 | mesh axes; the product must equal the device count |
| `--ga` | 1 | micro-batches per optimizer step |
| `--seq`, `--steps` | 1024, 23 | tokens per example; optimizer steps including warmup |
| `--scan` | off | MaxText's scanned decoder (its production default; tunix uses a Python loop) |
| `--opt` | `sgd` | `sgd` or `adamw`, matched across arms |
| `--explicit` | off | `shard_mode=explicit` — Explicit rather than Auto mesh axes |
| `--zero1` | off | `shard_optimizer_over_data`; implies `--explicit`; engine arm only |
| `--ring-of-experts`, `--ragged-sort` | off | MoE kernels; require `--ep > 1` |
| `--no-trace` | traces on | skip xprof — **required for any wall-clock number** |
| `--devices N` | all | use only the first N local devices |
| `PERF_PARITY_PROFILE_ROOT` | `./profiles` | where traces are written |

---

### Appendix B: Measurement notes

These are the traps that produce plausible wrong numbers rather than errors. Each was hit.

**Wall clock must come from `--no-trace` runs.** The profiler charges per dispatch, and the two
trainers dispatch very differently — at qwen3-0.6b/GA=8 the traces record **147.3 module
launches per step on the engine against 18.0 on `PeftTrainer`**. Both run nine substantial
kernels; the engine's other ~138 are small eager dispatches, each a separate host round trip.
Traced GA=8 wall clock runs 345–586 ms against 247–372 untraced, and inflates the arms
unevenly — a traced A/B **reverses the GA=8 ranking outright**. On the 35b model the same
overhead is at most 0.08%, because a 2.3 s step with ~14 dispatches gives it nothing to bite on.

**Per-kernel device times are comparable within a GA setting, not across one.** The same HLO
program hash measures 1.8–4.6 ms slower at GA=1 than at GA=8 in all three engine arms. Every
subtraction in §2.2 is taken within one GA column.

**Tracing lowers the engine's peak HBM by ~2.4 G, and only the engine's.** 12.73 G untraced
against 10.36 G traced at GA=8; both `PeftTrainer` arms are identical either way. Step count is
not the variable — re-running untraced at `--steps 6` reproduces the 23-step figures exactly.
The likely cause is dispatch depth (the engine runs further ahead of the device, and the
profiler's synchronization drains the queue), consistent with the engine-only incidence and the
~2.4 G size, but not verified directly. Memory figures come from `--no-trace` runs.

**Read TPU-busy off the `XLA Modules` line, not `XLA Ops`.** On a scanned MoE the Ops line sums
to roughly twice both the module time and the wall step, because ops inside the scan are
emitted underneath a fusion that already covers them.

**Take the maximum per-execution duration, never a mean or a total-over-steps.** Ragged sort
runs on SparseCore and floods the trace buffer (~1.3 M events against ~18 k at tp=2), dropping
most of the `XLA Modules` line; a clipped event then averages in as a fast step. `maybe_trace`
now passes base.yml's `enable_tpu_profiling_options` to `jax.profiler.trace`, which caps the
capture and keeps every execution; `--no-tpu-profiling-options` restores the raw behaviour.

**A bare `jax.sharding.Mesh(create_device_mesh(...), axes)` silently disables Zero-1.**
`_zero1_active` requires *all* `mesh.axis_types` to be `Explicit`, and that constructor leaves
them `Auto`. The arms build their mesh with `maxtext_utils.get_mesh_from_config(...)`, and
every engine arm prints a `zero1: ACTIVE | DECLINED (reason) | UNSUPPORTED` line — a declined
run is the baseline wearing the feature's name, which is invisible in a step time.

**The engine's own `fwd_bwd / update` split does not decompose the step.** `fwd_bwd` dispatches
asynchronously and the blocking wait lands inside `update()`, so at GA=1 the whole step appears
on the update side. Use the device figures.

**`enable_checkpointing=False` does not stop the engine writing a final checkpoint.** `close()`
ends in `save_checkpoint(..., force=True)` and the manager arms itself on `checkpoint_dir` being
non-empty. On the 35b model in f32 that is a ~140 G write per run, which filled this host's disk
and killed the first sweep. `engine_profile.py` now disarms the manager when the config says
checkpointing is off; the write lands after the timed loop either way.

---

**GRPO integration test:** `tests/post_training/integration/maxtext_engine_grpo_loss_test.py` — 1 passed in 51.67 s on the real checkpoint. Note it never calls `engine.compile()`, so it measures the eager path (237 ms/update vs 14 ms). Two things in it are now load-bearing: the batch is derived from the mesh rather than hard-coded, for the reason under change (1); and `matmul_precision=highest` is pinned, because the KL assertion compares log-probs from two code paths — Tunix's `compute_per_token_logps` for the reference against the engine's sharded forward for the policy — which at bf16 disagree by ~2e-2 on values near -12.6, and `low_var_kl` squares that into a KL of ~1.2e-4, an order of magnitude above the tolerance the assertion is trying to police.

**xprof traces for the (7)-(9) A/B**, engine arm only, `base/` = this fix's parent commit and `head/` = the fix, at the two shapes in "The host step path":

```
gs://chengnuojin-xprof/engine-hostpath-20260901/base/qwen3-0.6b-engine-fsdp1tp8/
gs://chengnuojin-xprof/engine-hostpath-20260901/head/qwen3-0.6b-engine-fsdp1tp8/
gs://chengnuojin-xprof/engine-hostpath-20260901/base/qwen3.5-35b-a3b-engine-scan-fsdp4tp2/
gs://chengnuojin-xprof/engine-hostpath-20260901/head/qwen3.5-35b-a3b-engine-scan-fsdp4tp2/
```

Traced, that A/B reads 271.4 → 92.8 ms and 2350.0 → 2315.2 ms. Compilation is inside these windows — the engine arm calls `compile()` under the trace on purpose — so read the steady-state region, not the whole trace.

**One bug found while measuring, not fixed here.** MaxText logs a different loss than it optimizes: `MetricsRecorder._record_metric` appends one entry per micro-step, no `aggregation_fn` is registered for `"loss"`, so `MetricsLogger._process_metrics` reduces it with `np.mean` — mean-of-means, the normalization change (4) deliberately avoids. On the ragged GA=4 batch the logged loss is `0.08643750101327896` while the gradient uses `-0.03790009766817093`; the sign disagrees. Gradients are unaffected. Left for a separate change since it is reporting-only and predates this PR.

title: Add scheduled-only label to allow running scheduled tests on PRs if required
body:
# Description

Tests marked `scheduled_only` (and the whole TPU7X suite) only run in the periodic scheduled CI, so regressions in them are only caught hours after a PR lands, and a PR author who knowingly touches that area has no way to validate it before merging.

This PR adds a `scheduled-only` PR label that re-runs the CI pipeline as if it were a scheduled run:

- `ci_pipeline.yml` now listens to the `pull_request: [labeled]` event. Every entry job (`analyze_code_changes`, `code_quality_check`, `docs_build_check`) is gated on the added label being `scheduled-only`, so adding any other label (`pull ready`, `gemini-review`, etc.) leaves all jobs skipped and costs no CI capacity.
- `is_scheduled_run` is set to true when the label is present, so the `not scheduled_only` pytest filter is dropped, `cpu-unit` installs torch-cpu, and coverage is uploaded under the `scheduled` flag — identical to a cron run.
- `analyze_code_changes.sh` gains a `FORCE_ALL_TESTS` escape hatch so a labeled PR runs every suite instead of only the ones matching the changed files.
- TPU7X tests, previously hard-skipped on PRs, run when the label is present.

`notify_failure` / `investigate_failure` deliberately stay `schedule`-only, so a failing labeled PR does not open or comment on tracking issues.

The label is opt-in: remove and re-add it to trigger another run.

title: upgrade tokamax floor to 0.0.14
body:
## Description

Upgrades `tokamax` to 0.0.14.

Per `docs/development/update_dependencies.md`, the source change is the floor in `base_requirements/requirements.txt` (`tokamax!=0.1.0` -> `tokamax>=0.0.14,!=0.1.0`) and the `generated_requirements/` locks were regenerated with the `seed-env` flow, the same way `bde759abd` (drjax) did it.

- Pre-training locks (`tpu`, `cuda12`) regenerated with JAX build commit `ab4c9b943c70bcb42baf4d379036a19c8aa2689d`
- Post-training lock regenerated with JAX build commit `52d5cb3893727451d0f695bfa6f8206cdd9492c7`
- `decoupled-requirements.txt` regenerated from the new GPU lock
- `requirements/requirements.txt`: stale `tokamax>=0.0.4` floor raised to `>=0.0.14`

Regenerating re-resolves each lock in full against the JAX seed and current PyPI, so the locks also carry the releases that landed since the last regeneration on 2026-08-31. `jax`, `jaxlib`, `jaxtyping`, `libtpu`, `flax`, `qwix` and `orbax-checkpoint` are unchanged; the largest unrelated move is `transformers 5.16.1 -> 5.17.0` and the rest are patch releases.

### Decoupled mode

The decoupled requirements stay pinned at `tokamax==0.0.12`. 0.0.14 still imports `xprof` at module scope (`tokamax/__init__.py` -> `tokamax/_src/benchmarking.py`), and `xprof` is filtered out of that environment, so every test reaching `maxtext.layers.moe` would fail to collect. The comment next to `PINNED_PACKAGES` records that this was re-checked against 0.0.14.

### Note for dependency owners: the xprof cap is ineffective

Pre-existing and deliberately not changed here. tokamax has required `xprof>=2.23.1` since 0.0.13, while the overrides cap it:

| File | Constraint |
| --- | --- |
| `extra_deps/tpu_overrides.txt` | `xprof<=2.23.0` |
| `extra_deps/cuda12_overrides.txt` | `xprof<=2.23.0` |
| `extra_deps/tpu_post_train_overrides.txt` | `xprof>=2.20.0,<=2.23.0` |
| generated TPU/GPU locks | `xprof>=2.20.0` |

uv `override-dependencies` *replace* a declared requirement rather than intersect with it, so during locking the cap silently wins and the locks keep `xprof>=2.20.0`. Overrides do not apply at install time, so installing any of these locks resolves `xprof` to 2.23.1 anyway to satisfy tokamax, which is what my test environment ended up with. The cap is therefore a no-op for real installs and the locked floor understates the true minimum. This surfaced when trying to re-resolve with every other package held at its current version, which fails with:

```
Because tokamax>=0.0.14 depends on xprof>=2.23.1
and your project depends on tokamax>=0.0.14 and xprof==2.20.0,
we can conclude that your project requirements are unsatisfiable.
```

Happy to lift the cap in a follow-up if that is the right call.

## Tests

Run on a v6e-8 against the regenerated TPU lock (`tokamax 0.0.14`, `jax 0.11.1`, `flax 0.12.9`, `libtpu 0.0.48`, `transformers 5.17.0`, `xprof 2.23.1`):

`tests/integration/tokamax_test.py` (v1/v2, bf16/fp8, EP1/EP2), `tests/integration/check_vma_test.py`, `tests/unit/tokamax_ring_attention_test.py`, `tests/unit/tokamax_splash_attention_mask_test.py`, `tests/unit/kernels_test.py`, `tests/unit/pallas_mosaic_tpu_v2_kernel_test.py`, `tests/unit/fused_moe_qwix_test.py`, `tests/unit/attention_test.py`, `tests/unit/moe_test.py`, `tests/gather_reduce_sc_test.py`, `tests/equiv_chunk_test.py`.

### Pre-existing failure, not caused by this change

`tests/unit/moe_test.py::QuantizedMoeTest::test_gmm_grad_equivalence_tokamax_v2_fp8_dynamic_ep4` fails with NaN gradients:

```
[PASS] output          | max_abs_diff: 3.418e-03 | relative_norm_diff: 6.529e-02
[FAIL] var_grad-wi_0   | max_abs_diff: nan       | relative_norm_diff: nan
[FAIL] var_grad-wi_1   | max_abs_diff: nan       | relative_norm_diff: nan
2/6 leaves exceed relative_norm_diff_threshold=0.22.
```

Swapping only the tokamax wheel in the same environment gives a byte-identical failure signature on `tokamax==0.0.13`, so this is a pre-existing gmm_v2 fp8-dynamic + EP4 issue, not a 0.0.14 regression. The `_ep1` variant of the same test and the `bf16_ep4` variant pass on both versions.

# Description

This PR is the fifth part of decomposing the XPK to Cluster Toolkit document migration. It focuses on updating our core infrastructure, training, and diagnostic documentation to use Cluster Toolkit (CTK) instead of the deprecated XPK launcher.

**Specifically, this PR updates the following areas:**
- **Pre-Training & Benchmarking:** Migrates the workload submission instructions in the pre-training and performance benchmarking guides from `xpk` to `gcluster`.
- **Diagnostics:** Updates cluster diagnostic tools and debugging documentation to reflect the new CTK environment and logs retrieval process.
- **Model Configs:** Adjusts documentation surrounding specific model configurations to ensure any cluster-specific flags align with the new CTK standards.

**Why this is being made:**
CTK is replacing XPK as the primary submission mechanism for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) workloads. This final PR completes the documentation migration initiated in PR #5175, ensuring all user guides now correctly point to the supported CTK stack.

Tested by scripts that run the `gcluster` commands provided in the documents, with results stored in a GCS bucket.

title: Disallow use_indexer config combinations that zero the entire training objective
body:
# Description

In DeepSeek-V4 Stage 2 (Lightning Indexer Warm-up: use_indexer=True, indexer_sparse_training=False), train.py intentionally sets xent_sum = 0.0 (lm_loss = 0.0) so main model parameters remain frozen while the indexer trains via indexer_loss scaled by indexer_loss_scaling_factor.

However, base.yml defaults both indexer_sparse_training to False and indexer_loss_scaling_factor to 0.0. Enabling use_indexer=True without overriding at least one of these flags zeroes both lm_loss and indexer_loss, running training steps with total_loss == 0.0 and zero gradients without error.

Reject configurations where use_indexer=True, indexer_sparse_training=False, and indexer_loss_scaling_factor <= 0.0 in validate_train_config and loss_fn, while permitting valid Stage 2 warm-up (indexer_loss_scaling_factor > 0.0) and Stage 3 sparse training (indexer_sparse_training=True).

title: Add sharding rules and mesh creation to m3 core
body:
# Description

Adds `m3/core/sharding.py`: logical-axis to `PartitionSpec` translation, plus
mesh creation over ICI and DCN.

Models never name a physical mesh axis. They name logical ones — `"embed"`,
`"heads"`, `"mlp"` — and a `Sharding` instance supplied at construction
translates them, so changing parallelism strategy means changing one class
rather than every model. Legacy instead carries 12 mesh axes and a ~105-entry
`logical_axis_rules` table; m3 starts with `dp`/`fsdp`/`tp`/`ep` and adds axes
as models need them.

Notes:

- `create_mesh(ici=..., dcn=...)` takes mappings rather than one keyword per
  axis, since the axis list is expected to grow. Unnamed axes are 1. Each
  mapping may carry one `-1`, because they resolve against different totals —
  devices-per-slice and slices.
- The single-slice path deliberately avoids `create_hybrid_device_mesh` with an
  all-ones DCN shape: that function requires every device to expose
  `slice_index`, which single-slice TPU and CPU devices lack, so it raises
  rather than degrading. A test pins the branch.
- `Sharding.__call__` rejects two dimensions of one tensor claiming the same
  mesh axis. Legacy tolerates this via Flax fallback rules (hence the duplicate
  keys in `logical_axis_rules`); m3 has no fallback, so it reports the conflict
  instead of emitting an invalid spec.
- `constrain` is activations-only — re-constraining a parameter after init
  collides with the training engine's deferred all-reduce and Zero-1 resharding.

Shortcomings:

- Sizes are passed directly; m3 config comes later.
- "Raise on an unknown logical axis" is a convention on the ABC, not enforced.
- Multi-slice tests stub the slice count and jax's placement function, as no
  testbed here spans slices. The arithmetic underneath is tested unmocked.
- `sharding.py` omits `__all__` (there are no star-imports in the repo);
  `rope.py` still has one, removed in a follow-up.

# Tests

`tests/unit/m3/sharding_test.py`, 54 tests. Multi-device cases are marked
`tpu_only` — without that marker the repo conftest treats them as `cpu_only`
and skips them on accelerator testbeds.

```
# CPU: 77 passed, 8 skipped
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu python3 -m pytest tests/unit/m3/ -q

# TPU v6e-8: 8 passed
python3 -m pytest tests/unit/m3/sharding_test.py -q -m tpu_only
```

title: DeepSeek V4 MTP Support
body:
# Description

Adds Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) support for DeepSeek V4, covering both the model layers and checkpoint conversion.

DeepSeek V4 carries a 4D residual stream `[batch, seq, mhc_expansion_rate, emb]` through the decoder (Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections), whereas V3 is plain 3D. Enabling MTP for V4 therefore means handling two orthogonal concerns at the prediction head:

- **Normalization**, which was already solved by the `normalize_y` flag added for V3 MTP in "Add separate final normalization for Multi-Token Prediction in DeepSeek models". This change reuses that mechanism rather than introducing a parallel one.
- **Collapsing the mHC streams**, which is V4-specific and is introduced here as a `reduce_mhc` flag on `apply_output_head`.

`NNXDecoder.__call__` now leaves the hidden state expanded and defers the collapse to `apply_output_head`, so the MTP block receives the full 4D state. Each MTP depth collapses it with its own learned hyper-connection head, applies its dedicated final norm, and then projects to logits with both normalization and reduction disabled. The unnormalized 4D state is what carries to the next depth:

```
NNXDecoder.__call__  ->  hidden_state = y          (stays 4D)
  main logits:  apply_output_head(hidden_state)     # reduce_mhc=True -> hc_head, then decoder_norm
  mtp_block(main_hidden_state=hidden_state)         # receives the full 4D state
      per depth k:  MTP layer (4D in -> 4D out)
                 -> mtp_layer.hc_head(...)          # 4D -> 3D, per-depth learned collapse
                 -> mtp_layer.final_norm(...)       # dedicated MTP RMSNorm
                 -> apply_output_head(..., normalize_y=False, reduce_mhc=False)
```

`reduce_mhc` defaults to `True`, which preserves existing behaviour for every current caller of `apply_output_head` (main logits, vocab tiling, and the vLLM adapter).

Two V4-specific details worth a reviewer's attention:

- `MultiTokenPredictionLayer` constructs a `DeepSeek4DecoderLayer` directly rather than using `transformer_layer_module`. With `scan_layers=True`, `get_decoder_layers()` returns a `DeepSeek4ScannableBlock` (a bundled HCA + CSA pair), which is not a single layer and cannot serve as an MTP layer.
- The per-depth `hc_head` is deliberately left unprefixed, unlike the other MTP submodules which are renamed to `mtp_{k}_*`, so that it matches the checkpoint key layout.

This also removes the config validation error that previously rejected `DecoderBlockType.DEEPSEEK4` in combination with MTP layers.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Stacked on #5000, which reworks DeepSeek V4 parameter mapping. The MTP conversion entries here are written against that refactor and depend on it, so #5000 should land first.

# Tests

**Unit tests**

- `tests/unit/param_mapping_test.py` — 35 passed. Adds three DeepSeek V4 MTP cases: the keys the MTP block contributes, that they disappear when `mtp_num_layers=0`, and a split/rejoin round-trip for the fused projection kernel.
- `tests/unit/multi_token_prediction_test.py` and `tests/unit/flop_calculation_test.py` — 84 passed, 9 skipped (skips unrelated to this change).

**Checkpoint conversion**

The MaxText-side keys generated for the MTP block were diffed against the `mtp_block` keys actually present in a converted DeepSeek V4 MTP checkpoint: an exact 45/45 match, no missing and no extra keys, for both `scan_layers=True` and `scan_layers=False`. That also confirms the MTP transformer layer carries a MoE gate bias but neither a compressor nor a hash-routing table, consistent with it being built with `compress_ratio=0` and `is_hash_routing=False`.

**End-to-end**

DeepSeek V4 284B on v5p-128 (64 devices), C4, `mtp_num_layers=1`, `mtp_eval_target_module=1`, `max_target_length=2048`, bf16, evaluating after each of 3 steps:

| Step | `mtp_acceptance_rate` | eval loss | perplexity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 79.09% | 2.234 | 9.338 |
| 1 | 79.12% | 2.234 | 9.338 |
| 2 | 79.13% | 2.234 | 9.337 |

An earlier measurement of this model gave a 74.9% acceptance rate. The improvement comes from #5226, which fixed restoration of checkpoint weights held outside the `params` collection; for DeepSeek V4 those include the MoE gate biases, whose absence degraded routing.

title: fix(elastic): Keep an abandoned setup attempt from leaking into the retry
body:
# Description

`train_loop()`'s initialization retry can use the results of a setup attempt it has already abandoned, leaving the run with a mesh from one topology and batch sizes from another. `pw-snp-4x1k-0827-3` hit this and died before its first step with

```
IndivisibleError: ... Mesh('data': 3, 'fsdp': 2048, ...), spec=P(('data', 'fsdp'), None) ...
array axis 0 is partitioned 6144 times, but the dimension size is 8192
```

It started on 3 slices, the fourth returned mid-setup, and the retry re-sized the config to 4 slices (batch 8192) while the first attempt kept running. That attempt finished first, and because `run_setup` was defined inside the loop and captured `setup_results`, `init_complete_event` and `devices` — all rebound on each retry — its late result landed in the new attempt's dict and set the new attempt's event. The main thread compiled the 3-slice mesh against the 4-slice batch.

- **Each attempt gets its own state.** `run_setup` is defined once and takes its results dict, events and devices as thread arguments, so a late result lands in a dict nobody reads.
- **The abandoned attempt is cancelled.** The retry sets its `cancel_event`; `setup_train_loop()` checks it before creating the data iterator and before restoring state. An attempt already inside the restore still finishes it — an in-flight Orbax restore cannot be stopped from here.
- **The mesh must match the config.** After setup, `train_loop()` retries if the mesh does not have `config.num_target_devices` devices.

FIXES: b/553546847

# Tests

**Unit.** New `tests/unit/train_setup_retry_test.py`: `test_abandoned_attempt_results_are_ignored` drives the real retry loop with a mocked `setup_train_loop()` where attempt 1 returns after attempt 2 started — it fails on the base branch (`['stale'] != ['current']`); `test_cancelled_setup_skips_data_and_restore` checks a cancelled setup creates no data iterator and restores nothing. 84 tests pass across `tests/unit/{train_setup_retry,elastic_utils,train_utils,goodput_utils}_test.py`.

**Hardware.** tpu7x `2x2x1` slices on `bodaborg-tpu7x-spot-sps`, llama3.1-8b, `elastic_backup_kind=snapshot`, restoring an 8B checkpoint at step 180, on the incident's `20260826_3ae3` images with the changed files mounted over them (base branch vs. this branch, nothing else differs). One slice was SIGSTOPped before MaxText started and SIGKILLed once the restore began, so it rejoined while the first attempt was still restoring.

| run | base branch | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 3 slices (Sep 21) | `IndivisibleError`, 16 vs 24, exit 134 | steps 181–219 on 3 slices, exit 0 |
| 3 slices (Sep 22) | `IndivisibleError`, 16 vs 24, exit 134 | steps 181–219, `jit_train_step … load_slices: 3`, exit 0 |
| 2 slices (Sep 22) | trains on the stale 1-slice mesh, `load_slices: 1`, exit 0 | `load_slices: 2`, exit 0 |

The 2-slice pair shows the silent form: 16 divides by 8, so there is no crash and the run trains on one slice while reporting `active_slices: 2`, a count that comes from the elastic manager rather than the mesh.

title: Dual-Pathway Cosmos3MoTDecoderLayer
body:
# Description

Adds the **Cosmos 3 Core Dual-Attention Operator (`CosmosDualAttention`)** and the **Dual-Pathway Mixture-of-Transformers Decoder Layer (`Cosmos3MoTDecoderLayer`)** in Flax NNX to MaxText.

### Context & Motivation
Cosmos 3 uses a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture with two parallel transformer towers that maintain independent weights (projections, QK norms, pre/post RMSNorms, and MLPs) while sharing a single fused attention step:
- **Understanding pathway (`und`)**: processes text/prompt tokens using sample-isolated causal self-attention.
- **Generation pathway (`gen`)**: processes continuous video/multimodal latents using sample-isolated full bidirectional attention that also cross-attends to the understanding stream's keys and values.

### Implementation Details
1. **Dual-Pathway Packed Attention (`src/maxtext/layers/cosmos_attention.py`)**:
   - `CosmosPackingMetadata` & `build_cosmos_packing_metadata`: constructs cumulative sample boundary offsets (`causal_q_offsets`, `full_q_offsets`, `sample_kv_offsets`) and stream scatter/gather index maps (`packed_und_token_indexes`, `packed_gen_token_indexes`).
   - `unpack_streams` & `reinterleave_streams`: splits interleaved packed token sequences into understanding/generation streams and merges outputs back into global packed sequence order.
   - `compute_3d_mrope_cos_sin` & `apply_rotary_pos_emb`: implements 3D Multimodal Rotary Position Embeddings (3D M-RoPE) across temporal, height, and width sections.
   - `causal_understanding_attention` & `full_generative_attention`: supports `dot_product`, `flash`, and `splash` attention backends with strict cross-sample isolation masks (`build_causal_understanding_mask`, `build_full_generative_mask`, and Tokamax Splash mask compilation).
   - `CosmosDualAttention`: Flax NNX module encapsulating independent understanding and generation projections (`q_proj`/`k_proj`/`v_proj`/`o_proj` and `*_gen`), independent QK RMSNorms, and optional cross-pathway `k_norm_und_for_gen`.

2. **MoT Decoder Layer & Per-Tower MLPs (`src/maxtext/models/cosmos3.py`)**:
   - `Cosmos3MLP`: per-tower feed-forward block supporting both gated SwiGLU (`hidden_act="silu"`, Qwen3 backbone) and ungated squared-ReLU (`hidden_act="relu2"`, Nemotron backbone).
   - `Cosmos3MoTDecoderLayer`: composes `CosmosDualAttention` with independent understanding and generation towers:
     - Understanding pathway: `input_layernorm`, `to_q`, `to_k`, `to_v`, `to_out`, `norm_q`, `norm_k`, `post_attention_layernorm`, `mlp`.
     - Generation pathway: `input_layernorm_moe_gen`, `add_q_proj`, `add_k_proj`, `add_v_proj`, `to_add_out`, `norm_added_q`, `norm_added_k`, `post_attention_layernorm_moe_gen`, `mlp_moe_gen`.
   - Exposes `diffusers`-canonical parameter names (`to_q`, `add_q_proj`, `to_add_out`, `norm_added_q`, etc.) as zero-copy property aliases onto `self_attn` so checkpoint loaders and parity tests can address either naming convention without duplicating parameters in the NNX graph.

This label is used for administrative purposes. Please do not add it manually.

title: feat(quantization): add native FP8 inference (serve_fp8_weight) for DenseGeneral and GMM v2
body:
# Description

Implements native FP8 inference (`quantization="serve_fp8_weight"`) for Qwen3.5 (and other FP8-quantized architectures) to execute forward passes directly using quantized FP8 weights without on-the-fly dequantization ([b/557372531](http://b/557372531)).

Previously, weights stored/loaded in FP8 were dequantized on-the-fly to BF16 prior to compute, causing substantial memory bandwidth and runtime overhead during inference and RL rollouts. This change allows weights to stay in FP8 and compute directly via native FP8 GEMMs across DenseGeneral (supporting per-tensor, per-channel, and block-wise scaling) and RoutedMoE (supporting both tokamax v2 FP8 GMM and vLLM fused MoE via `tpu_inference`).

---

# Benchmark & Performance Results

Evaluated on **TPU v6e-8** (8 chips, GhostLite) using the per-tensor quantized `qwen3.5-35b-a3b-fp8` checkpoint (`/dev/shm/maxtext_qwen3.5_35b_fp8_pertensor_v3`), running a standalone autoregressive decode forward loop simulating RL rollout forward inference (batch size = 1, sequence length = 64 tokens, `scan_layers=True`, `attention="dot_product"`).

### Performance Summary

| Metric | Baseline (`quantization=""`) | Diff (`quantization="serve_fp8_weight"`) | Delta / Speedup |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Average Forward Step Time (15 steps)** | **471.59 ms** (±3.07 ms) | **259.80 ms** (±3.25 ms) | **1.81x faster (-45.0% latency)** |
| **Step 0 (JIT Compilation)** | 5.12 s | 1.32 s | **3.88x faster compile** |
| **Output Logits Finite** | Yes (all finite) | Yes (all finite) | Parity verified |

title: [Qwen3.5] Mask left-padding tokens in Qwen3NextGatedDeltaNet and guar…
body:
…d l2norm against singular backward gradients

# Description

### Summary

In **Qwen3.5-35B-A3B** (and hybrid **GatedDeltaNet (GDN)** linear-attention models), batch training and rollout parity evaluation under **left-padding** (`decoder_segment_ids == 0`) suffer from two coupled forward and backward defects, plus a pre-existing unsharded forward-pass crash on `main`:

1. **Forward Pass Recurrent State Corruption (Causal Conv1D Boundary Bleed)**:
   - `Qwen3NextGatedDeltaNet` applies a 1D causal depthwise convolution (`self.conv1d`, kernel size $K = 4$) across time to `qkv = [q, k, v]`.
   - On a left-padded sequence with $P$ pad tokens ($[t_0, \dots, t_{P-1}]$ where `decoder_segment_ids == 0`), unmasked pad positions produce non-zero `qkv` projections. When the causal window slides over the first valid prompt token $t_P$: $$\text{conv\_out}[t_P] = W_0\,\text{qkv}[t_P] + W_1\,\text{qkv}[t_{P-1}] + W_2\,\text{qkv}[t_{P-2}] + W_3\,\text{qkv}[t_{P-3}]$$ the non-zero pad tokens $t_{P-1}, t_{P-2}, t_{P-3}$ bleed directly into $k[t_P]$ and $v[t_P]$.
   - Because the Gated Delta Rule recurrence updates state via $S_t = S_{t-1}(I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top) + \beta_t v_t k_t^\top$, polluting $t_P$ permanently corrupts the persistent recurrent matrix $S_t$ across the entire sequence in all 30 GDN layers.

2. **Backward Pass Singular Jacobian & Exponential Gradient Explosion**:
   - When padding activations are zeroed ($x = \mathbf{0}$), downstream normalization layers (`l2norm` on $q, k$ and per-head gated `RMSNorm` on $v$) evaluate at $x = \mathbf{0}$, where the local Jacobian is: $$J(\mathbf{0}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\,I = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10^{-6}}}\,I = 1000\,I$$
   - Each GDN layer applies both `l2norm` ($\text{gain} = 1000$) and gated `RMSNorm` ($\text{gain} = 1000$), yielding a per-layer backward cotangent amplification of $1000 \times 1000 = 10^6$ on padding positions, and $(10^6)^{30} = 10^{180}$ across $L = 30$ GDN layers—overflowing IEEE-754 `float32` ($> 3.4 \times 10^{38}$) and destabilizing training gradients.

3. **Pre-existing Unsharded GDN `NoneType` Crash on `main` (`src/maxtext/models/qwen3.py:1143`)**:
   - `jax_chunk_gated_delta_rule` returns `None` for `next_recurrent_state` when called without an `initial_state`. On the unsharded (`self.mesh is None`) code path in train mode, `next_recurrent_state = next_recurrent_state.astype(cfg.dtype)` unconditionally dereferences `None` (`AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'astype'`), breaking `test_gated_delta_net_structure` and `test_gated_delta_net_full` on `origin/main`.

---

### Solution (Isolated Changes in This PR)

1. **`src/maxtext/models/qwen3.py` (`Qwen3NextGatedDeltaNet.__call__`)**:
   - **Before `self.conv1d` (Forward Boundary Isolation)**: Zero `qkv` where `decoder_segment_ids == 0` so pad tokens contribute exact `0.0` into the sliding convolution window of the first real token.
   - **After `self.conv1d` (Internal Cotangent Isolation)**: Zero `conv_out` where `decoder_segment_ids == 0` to block internal backward cotangents from propagating into `self.conv1d.kernel`.
   - **Before Recurrence (`query`, `key`, `value`, `g`)**: Mask `query` alongside `key`, `value`, and `g` where `decoder_segment_ids == 0`.
   - **After `self.out_proj` (Output Cotangent Severance)**: Zero `output` where `decoder_segment_ids == 0` before returning from `Qwen3NextGatedDeltaNet.__call__`, forcing incoming backward cotangents $\bar{\text{output}}$ on padding positions to be identically `0.0` so downstream loss gradients never enter `RMSNorm`, `l2norm`, or `conv1d` on padding tokens.
   - **Guard `next_recurrent_state` cast**: Check `if next_recurrent_state is not None:` before calling `.astype(cfg.dtype)` on the unsharded path.
2. **`src/maxtext/layers/normalizations.py` (`l2norm`)**:
   - Guard `l2norm` against zero-norm vectors using JAX's double-`jnp.where` pattern (`safe_norm_sq = jnp.where(is_zero, 1.0, norm_sq)`) so zeroed rows have exact `0.0` forward output and exact `0.0` backward gradient without $1/\sqrt{\epsilon}$ amplification.
3. **`tests/unit/qwen3_next_vs_reference_test.py`**:
   - Add `test_gated_delta_net_left_padding_invariance_and_gradients` verifying: 1. Exact `0.0` outputs on left-padded positions (`decoder_segment_ids == 0`). 2. Exact forward numerical invariance (`rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5`) between unpadded sequences and left-padded sequences with high-amplitude padding noise. 3. Strictly finite backward gradients (`jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(grads))`) with exact `0.0` gradients on padding positions.

FIXES: b/563191139
BUGS: b/563502305

# Tests

- **Local Unit Tests (`pytest tests/unit/qwen3_next_vs_reference_test.py` on CPU)**:

| Test Case | `origin/main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `test_gated_delta_net_structure` | FAIL (`AttributeError: 'NoneType'`) | **PASS** | | `test_gated_delta_net_full` | FAIL (`AttributeError: 'NoneType'`) | **PASS** | | `test_gated_delta_net_left_padding_invariance_and_gradients` | N/A (new test) | **PASS** | | `test_chunk_gated_delta_rule_logic`, `test_l2norm`, `test_rms_norm_gated`, `test_qwen3_next_rms_norm`, `test_full_attention_dot_product` | PASS | **PASS** | | `test_qwen3_next_sparse_moe_block` | FAIL (pre-existing unrelated MoE issue) | FAIL (untouched / out of scope) |

- **Pre-commit Linters**:
  - `uvx pre-commit run --files src/maxtext/layers/normalizations.py src/maxtext/models/qwen3.py tests/unit/qwen3_next_vs_reference_test.py` (`codespell`, `pylint`, `pyink`) passes with 0 errors.
- **Teacher-Forced Rollout Parity (`Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`)**:
  - Median per-token logprob discrepancy $|d\log p|$ reduced from **0.1235 → 0.0073**.
  - Truncated Importance Sampling out-of-bounds ratio (`tis/is_oob_ratio`) on left-padded batches reduced from **97.82%–100.0% → 31.25%–46.88%** standalone (and **73.8% → 6.94%** end-to-end with MoE router replay).
- **Distributed Multi-Step GRPO Stability (`v5p`)**:
  - Forward and backward passes remain 100% finite with well-behaved gradient norms across 50-step GRPO RL convergence runs.

title: Add elastic reshard and recovery to the MaxText pre-train loop.
body:
Add elastic reshard and recovery to the MaxText pre-train loop.

Second CL in the elastic-snapshot stack. Builds on the utilities added in the
previous CL to make the pre-train loop survive a slice going down and pick up a
slice coming back, without falling back to a GCS checkpoint restore.

## What this adds

`trainers/pre_train/train.py`

*   `save_snapshot()` — writes an in-memory (host) snapshot of the NNX model
    and optimizer state through the Orbax Pathways `Snapshotter`.
*   `recover()` — the reshard path. Waits for a viable slice set, mutates the
    config to the new topology, cancels in-flight checkpoint saves, rebuilds
    mesh/model/optimizer via `setup_train_loop()`, re-jits the train and eval
    steps on the new mesh, and then restores state from one of three sources in
    priority order:
    1.  the still-live device state (scale-up: device-to-device reshard),
    2.  the in-memory host snapshot (scale-down: HBM was lost),
    3.  the persistent GCS checkpoint (last resort).
*   `recreate_dataloaders()` — rebuilds the data/eval iterators and loader for
    the new mesh after a reshard.
*   Training loop: each step now runs under a `pathwaysutils` watchdog, checks
    for newly available inactive slices, and catches `JaxRuntimeError` /
    `ScaleUpSignalError`. The two recovery kinds are routed separately —
    `is_scale_up` sends the scale-up case down the device-to-device path with
    `active_state=` set, while a slice failure goes down the snapshot path.
    Conflating them was the bug that made scale-up events restore from a stale
    snapshot.
*   `_safe_replace()` — NNX's `replace_by_pure_dict` raises on any key present
    in the restored pure dict but absent from the freshly built state. GCS
    checkpoints carry `rngs`/`aqt` subtrees a scratch `m_state` does not have,
    so the restore is filtered to the intersection first.
*   The TE MoE capacity-overflow window is now gated on the step having
    actually produced metrics. A recovered step `continue`s before
    `training_loop_iteration()` returns, so the previous unconditional read of
    `metrics[...]` would have hit an unbound local on the first recovery.

`utils/train_utils.py`

*   `setup_train_loop()` gains `restore_checkpoint` and `checkpoint_manager`.
    `recover()` re-enters `setup_train_loop()` with the existing manager and
    `restore_checkpoint=False`, so it rebuilds the mesh and model without
    reopening a second `CheckpointManager` or reading the checkpoint back.
*   `create_checkpoint_manager()` now registers the colocated-Python array
    handler *before* constructing the manager and passes
    `array_metadata_store=None`. In Pathways colocated-Python mode sharding and
    storage are managed centrally by the controller via TensorStore, so Orbax's
    per-process `array_metadatas/` files are redundant. Registering late left
    `PyTreeCheckpointHandler` holding the default store, which produced a 600s
    stall waiting for `process_index=0` to create `array_metadatas/` and then
    `ValueError: No ArrayMetadata found for process_index=0` during recovery.
*   `replicate_single_device_sharded_arrays()` /
    `restore_original_shardings()` — the snapshotter requires mesh-sharded
    inputs, so single-device leaves are replicated before save/load and put
    back on their original shardings afterwards. PRNG-key leaves are unwrapped
    with `key_data`/`wrap_key_data` around the `device_put`.
*   `validate_train_config()` rejects `elastic_enabled` together with emergency
    or multi-tier checkpointing; those paths assume a fixed slice count.

`common/checkpointing.py`

*   `cancel_checkpoint_manager()` — detaches in-flight async save and finalize
    threads so a reshard doesn't block on a save targeting the old mesh.
*   `load_state_if_possible()` distinguishes "no checkpoint manager" from "no
    checkpoints found". `recover()` calls it with a manager that may be None.

`common/train_state_nnx.py`

*   `_strip_rng_state()` handles an `nnx.State` input via
    `nnx.split_state(..., nnx.Not(nnx.RngState), ...)`, not just plain dicts.

title: Add in-memory elastic snapshot utilities for Pathways multi-slice training.
body:
Add in-memory elastic snapshot utilities for Pathways multi-slice training.

Elastic training recovers from slice loss by restoring the most recent Orbax
checkpoint from GCS, and that read dominates recovery time at large multi-slice
scale. Surviving slices already hold a complete replica of the model state, so
recovery can be served from host and device memory instead.

Add the utility layer this requires to `elastic_utils`. `maybe_snapshot_state`
and `restore_resharded_state` capture and reshard either a `TrainStateNNX` or a
Linen train state across a mutated device mesh, `wait_for_devices_placed` polls
for device placement while slices join or leave, and `mutate_config_for_topology`
and `recalculate_batch_sizes` adapt batch sizing to the surviving topology.
Slice-count recording becomes non-fatal so a failed health check cannot abort a
training step.

Add `elastic_snapshot_interval` and `elastic_new_slice_check_period`, and raise
the `elastic_timeout_seconds` and `elastic_max_retries` defaults to values
validated during multi-slice scale testing. Resolve the slice count before the
hardware-dependent configuration block so elastic startup settles the topology
before device counts are derived.

Pin `pathwaysutils` to the revision that supplies the snapshot entry points
these helpers call.

Nothing calls the new helpers yet. The training loop integration follows in a
subsequent change.

title: Support vLLM mamba prefix caching in the Qwen3 GDN layer
body:
## Problem

Under vLLM's mamba prefix caching (`mamba_cache_mode="align"`), a Qwen3.5 rollout on the MaxText-native path dies on the first decode step:

```
File "maxtext/models/qwen3.py", line 913, in __call__
  recurrent_state, conv_state = active_cache.get_gdn_states()
AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'get_gdn_states'
```

`Qwen3NextGatedDeltaNet` decides whether vLLM is driving paged state by sniffing for one field:

```python
use_paged_state = (
    ... and getattr(attention_metadata, "mamba_state_indices", None) is not None and ...
)
```

But align mode is precisely the mode where tpu-inference stops populating it (`tpu_inference/runner/tpu_runner.py:3220-3246`):

```python
# In align mode (prefix caching), mamba state indices are derived on-device
# from the block tables, so mamba_state_indices is None.
if (self.kv_cache_config.has_mamba_layers and getattr(
        self.cache_config, "mamba_cache_mode", "none") != "align"):
    ...  # build mamba_state_indices
else:
    mamba_state_indices = None
```

So `use_paged_state` goes False and the layer falls through to the MaxEngine branch, calling `get_gdn_states()` on the 2-tuple of paged state arrays vLLM handed it.

## Change

Resolve the slots from the mamba block table when `mamba_state_indices` is absent.

Align mode needs the read and write slots to **differ**: a request resumes from the block covering its last already-computed token and writes to the block covering its last token, so a later request hitting that cached prefix can pick up the checkpoint. `run_jax_gdn_attention` already takes `read_state_indices` for exactly this (`tpu_inference/layers/common/gdn_attention.py:50`) — the vLLM path passes it, MaxText did not, so read == write. New `_mamba_block_table_slots` computes both and the call now forwards `read_state_indices=`.

`mamba_block_size` lives on vLLM's `cache_config`, which the layer has no handle on, so the adapter passes it down as a new `gdn_mamba_block_size` config key (0 when not in align mode). `generate_maxtext_config` already does this kind of vLLM→MaxText translation for sharding and MoE padding.

Non-align behaviour is unchanged: the `mamba_state_indices` branch is the same code as before, and `gdn_mamba_block_size` defaults to 0.

## Testing

`tests/unit/qwen3_gdn_mamba_slots_test.py`, 3 passed (CPU backend). Covers the read/write split across a block boundary, clamping into the rank-local range, and per-DP-rank slicing of the block table. The first case is inherently a regression test for the old behaviour — it expects read block 11 and write block 12 for the same request.

title: ci(cpu-unit): run the unit tests on 4 virtual CPU devices
body:
# Description

Follow-up to the discussion on the last round of test fixes: turn `cpu-unit` into the job that catches multi-device sharding bugs, instead of letting them reach accelerator runners.

- `tests/conftest.py` auto-marks any test without an explicit hardware marker as `cpu_only`, and the accelerator jobs deselect `cpu_only` -- so **`cpu-unit` is the only job that runs that bulk**.
- It runs on a single device, where two whole classes of bug pass for the wrong reason:
  - a test whose batch is smaller than its mesh (1 row "divides" 1 device), and
  - a test that relies on ambient flax `axis_rules` it never entered (everything resolves to unsharded, so context-parallel code paths are silently skipped).
- Both only fail once 2+ devices are visible. Four rounds have now reached `main` this way: #5133, #5134, #5286, #5287 -- all authored after the failures were found on a 4-device runner rather than in the PR that introduced them.
- This sets `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=4` for the `cpu-unit` flavor only. No new job, no new runner, no accelerators: the CPU backend simply exposes 4 virtual devices in one process.

# Tests

Tested on recent main branch, running the exact `cpu-unit` selection (`-m "cpu_only and not post_training and not integration_test" --ignore=tests/post_training`):

| | failed | passed | skipped | time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 devices | 25 | 2003 | 1393 | 15m08s |
| 1 device (today) | 25 | 1965 | 1431 | 13m14s |

- **The two failure sets are identical** - nothing fails at 4 devices that does not already fail at 1.
- **38 tests that currently skip themselves now execute** - the ones guarded by `if len(devices) < 2: self.skipTest(...)`. That is the point of the change, and worth knowing: a few of those have never run anywhere.
- Cost is ~2 minutes of wall time. `linux-x86-n2-32` (32 vCPU / 128 GB) has plenty of headroom; the 4 devices share host RAM.

Reproduce either column locally with:

    JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=4 python -m pytest \
      -m "cpu_only and not post_training and not integration_test" --ignore=tests/post_training tests/

If you would rather keep a single-device signal as well, I am happy to respin this as a separate `cpu-unit-multidevice` flavor instead of changing `cpu-unit` in place - that needs entries in the coordinator's per-flavor maps plus a job in `ci_pipeline.yml`, so I went with the smaller change first.

title: Fix TE EP capacity sizing for gradient accumulation
body:
# Description

Fix TransformerEngine EP buffer capacity sizing when gradient accumulation is enabled.

Previously, EP bootstrap used the entire accumulated batch to calculate `max_tokens_per_rank`. Each MoE invocation processes only one microbatch, so this unnecessarily increased receive-buffer and staging-buffer capacity with GA, potentially causing OOMs.

This change:
- Divides the loaded batch size by `gradient_accumulation_steps`.
- Preserves sufficient capacity for model initialization and larger evaluation batches.
- Validates GA and FSDP/EP batch divisibility.
- Leaves TE’s receive-capacity calculation and routing headroom unchanged.

For a workload with 6 sequences per GPU and sequence length 4096, the token bound now remains 24,576 tokens/rank regardless of GA.

This addresses EP overprovisioning, not separate XLA buffer-lifetime memory growth.

# Tests

- Added and passed 10 CPU unit tests with mocked TE bootstrap, covering:
  - GA=1, 2, 3, 16, and 32.
  - Larger, smaller, and disabled evaluation batches.
  - Expanded loaded batches and initialization sizing.
  - Invalid batch sizes and GA values.
  - Bootstrap caching and non-TE configurations.
- Passed Pyink formatting and `git diff --check`.
- Tested the same sizing change on a 16-GPU small DeepSeek workload with 5 layers, 128 experts, EP=4, and FSDP=4. GA=2, GA=3, and GA=16 all completed 15 training steps. EP receive capacity remained 393,216 slots/rank.
- Workload logs are internal and are not linked publicly.

Run the unit tests from the repository root in a MaxText development environment:

    DECOUPLE_GCLOUD=TRUE PYTHONPATH=src \
      python -m unittest discover \
      -s tests/unit -p te_moe_bootstrap_test.py -v

title: Make retry_when_tokens_dropped memory-neutral
body:
# Description

Enabling `retry_when_tokens_dropped` currently costs **+2.669 GiB/device of peak HBM (+4.9%)** and **+59 full-mesh all-reduces per step**, measured by AOT `train_compile` A/B on DeepSeek-v3-671B at `tpu7x-1024` (MLPerf flag set, only this flag differing). Neither cost is inherent to the feature. This PR removes both, bringing the flag's overhead down to **+10.6 MiB (+0.019%)** and **one** all-reduce.

| per-device | baseline | `retry_when_tokens_dropped=true` | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| generated_code | 0.4262 G | 0.4296 G | +3.5 MiB |
| argument | 7.3327 G | 7.3327 G | 0 |
| output | 7.3326 G | 7.3326 G | 0 |
| alias | 7.3326 G | 7.3326 G | **0** |
| temp | 46.8720 G | 46.8790 G | +7.1 MiB |
| **peak HBM** | **54.6309 G** | **54.6412 G** | **+10.6 MiB (+0.019%)** |

`may-alias` entries: 182 in both. Collectives: all-reduce 44 → 45, all-gather 141 → 141, reduce-scatter 24 → 24. The 58-trip MoE forward scan gains 18 instructions and **zero** collectives.

## 1. Keep the state donated by rolling the step back in-graph

The replay needs the pre-step state to still be live, which `get_functional_train_with_signature` arranged by setting `donate_argnums=()` whenever the flag was on. That dropped all 182 `input_output_alias` entries and paid for an un-aliased copy of the whole train state on *every* step to cover a rare event — the entire 2.669 GiB.

Instead the step always runs and discards its own update when an overflow is detected (`_rollback_on_overflow`): an elementwise `jnp.where(has_moe_overflow, old, new)` over the state leaves, which XLA folds into the existing optimizer-update fusions (+154 selects, no new buffers). The donated buffers are still written in place, and the returned state is bit-identical to the input whenever an overflow occurred, so `training_loop_iteration` replays straight from it — no second copy of the state is ever live, and the explicit `x.delete()` / `gc.collect()` dance it used to need is gone.

Two details:
- The dropless replay model sows a compile-time-constant `False`, so the select folds away entirely in the replay executable — that path pays nothing.
- Typed PRNG keys are skipped by the select (`jax.dtypes.extended` values aren't selectable). Leaving them advanced is harmless: the replay needs *a* valid key, not the original one.

## 2. Reduce the overflow flag once per model, not once per layer

`permute()` did `jax.lax.psum(local_overflow, tuple(mesh.axis_names))` — one `replica_groups=(1,1024)` all-reduce inside the 58-trip forward MoE scan, plus one for MTP, for a flag nothing in the layer consumes. It is only sown for the host-side retry decision. XLA cannot combine these with the pre-existing in-loop psum, which is only over `fsdp`.

`permute()` now returns the unreduced per-device flag, `sparse_matmul`'s `shard_map` emits it with `out_specs=P(tuple(mesh.axis_names))` (one element per device), and `loss_fn` does a single `jnp.any` for the whole model. `collect_intermediates_by_suffix` grows a `ravel` argument because flattening the mesh-sharded flag array would otherwise force a reshard.

The one new all-reduce is a `u32[] reduce_or` in `main._spmd`, outside every scan.

## 3. Reject `retry_when_tokens_dropped` with `enable_diloco`

The dropless replay executable is only built off the plain NNX train state. Under DiLoCo there is nothing to replay with, so with the in-graph rollback the step would discard its update on every overflow and silently make no progress. Now a config error.

# Tests

- **AOT A/B** (the numbers above): `train_compile` on `deepseek3-671b`, `compile_topology=tpu7x-1024`, MLPerf flag set, with and without `retry_when_tokens_dropped=true`. Peak HBM = `generated_code + argument + output - alias + temp` from `CompiledMemoryStats`; collective and `may-alias` counts from the optimized HLO.
- **New unit tests** in `tests/unit/train_nnx_test.py`: `test_state_is_rolled_back_on_overflow` asserts every returned state leaf is bit-identical to the input when the flag is set, and `test_state_advances_without_overflow` guards it from passing vacuously.
- `tests/unit/maxtext_utils_test.py::TestGetFunctionalTrainWithSignature` updated — donation now stays on with the flag.
- `pytest tests/unit/train_nnx_test.py tests/unit/maxtext_utils_test.py` (CPU): 136 passed, 9 skipped.
- `pytest tests/unit/moe_test.py -k "retry or force_dropless or overflow_detection"` (TPU v5, 4 chips): 4 passed.
- Full `pytest tests/unit/moe_test.py` (TPU v5): 6 failed, 34 passed, 53 skipped. All 6 failures are pre-existing — verified by re-running those node ids at `c8f300c7e` with this diff stashed, identical result. They all raise `AssertionError: lhs_scale requires lhs quantization to engage ... hardware supports fp8/int8 matmul`, i.e. the fp8/tokamax tests can't run on this TPU generation.
- `pre-commit run --files <changed>`: codespell, pylint, pyink, mdformat all pass.

**Not run:** an end-to-end training workload. The claim here is about compiled memory and collective counts, which the AOT A/B measures directly; a convergence/throughput run on the 671B config would be worth doing before this goes out for review.

title: Fix inference decoding query heads rule mapping to include autoregressive axis
body:
# Description

Fixes two independent bugs causing cudnn_flash_jax attention failures during autoregressive inference:

1. Query/KV batch-dimension mismatch: query and key/value can arrive with different batch sizes at the cuDNN flash attention call (e.g. KV cache batch reduced to 1 while query keeps the full batch size). This is handled defensively in attention_op.py regardless of sharding config.
2. Missing autoregressive axis mapping for query heads: in inference.yml, activation_kv_heads was already sharded along the autoregressive mesh axis, but activation_heads (query) was not — an inconsistency in the logical axis rules, fixed independently in the config.

Fix:
- src/maxtext/configs/inference/inference.yml: add 'autoregressive' to the activation_heads logical axis rule so query heads are sharded consistently with KV heads under autoregressive parallelism.
- src/maxtext/layers/attention_op.py:
  - Move validate_gpu_flash_attention and KV dequantization earlier (before check_attention_inputs) for the cudnn_flash_jax path.
  - Add _align_qkv_for_cudnn_flash, which broadcasts key/value along the batch dimension to match query's batch size when KV has batch size 1 (raises ValueError for any other mismatch).
  - In cudnn_jax_flash_attention, broadcast the computed autoregressive lengths array to match the query batch size when it was reduced to length 1.


# Tests

- tests/unit/attention_test.py: new CudnnFlashJaxInferenceTest covering _align_qkv_for_cudnn_flash (broadcast success + invalid-mismatch error) and that autoregressive q_seqlen/kv_seqlen are broadcast correctly in cudnn_jax_flash_attention.

title: fix(router replay test): size the data batch by device count
body:
# Description

- `per_device_batch_size` is **per device**: the real batch is that number times the device count, and the mesh shards the batch axis across every device.
- These tests use it as if it were the whole batch, building 1 or 2 rows. On a 4-device host the fsdp axis then tries to split 1 row four ways and the test dies with `IndivisibleError: array axis 0 is partitioned 4 times, but the dimension size is 1`.
- Batch size is incidental to what they assert (which experts the router replays), so the batch just needs to fit the mesh.
- CI has never caught this: these tests are auto-marked `cpu_only`, so only the single-device `cpu-unit` job runs them, where 1 row divides by 1 device fine.
- Fix: derive the row count from the config (`per_device_batch_size * jax.device_count()`) instead of reusing the per-device number, in the two batch-building helpers and the tests that build `forced_routed_experts`. Single-device behaviour is unchanged.

The seven tests affected are `test_loss_fn_with_forced_routed_experts`, ..._gemma4`, `..._scanned_qwen3_5`, `..._scanned_mixtral`, `test_different_replays_give_different_losses_unscanned`, and `test_per_layer_routing_is_not_broadcast_{scanned,unscanned}`.

# Tests

Reproduce the failure on `main` and the fix on this branch with:

    XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=4 python -m pytest tests/unit/router_replay_test.py

Verified on 4x AMD Instinct MI355X (ROCm 10, jax 0.11.1): the seven tests fail on `main` with the `IndivisibleError` above and pass on this branch. Full file passes in both environments that matter -- 4 devices (35 passed, 1 skipped) and a single CPU device (35 passed, 1 skipped), the latter being what `cpu-unit` runs today.

title: Train & Eval on entire dataset when pdbs < 1
body:
# Description

This PR fixes a bug where data was silently dropped when running with fractional per-device batch sizes (`per_device_batch_size < 1.0` or `eval_per_device_batch_size < 1.0`). In the past, the dataloader loaded at least one sample per device, but `loss_fn` truncated the input batch down to `micro_batch_size_to_train_on` or `micro_batch_size_to_eval_on`, discarding the remaining samples. With this change, the slicing logic is removed, and all loaded samples are processed across microbatches using gradient accumulation during training and forward-only metric accumulation during evaluation.

### Why This Solution
Instead of discarding data, setting `per_device_batch_size < 1.0` is treated as implicit microbatch accumulation:
- For training, gradient accumulation is automatically computed over `num_microbatches = global_batch_size_to_load // micro_batch_size_to_train_on`. All loaded samples are processed across microbatches and accumulated into the gradients.
- For evaluation, a dedicated forward-only scan loop (`_fractional_batch_eval`) processes each microbatch and aggregates metrics without performing unnecessary backpropagation.
- No data is thrown away, batch size calculations are consistent, and throughput matches the loaded dataset volume.

# Tests

Added unit tests to verify batch sizing calculations and microbatch accumulation:
- `tests/unit/pyconfig_test.py`:
  - `test_calculate_global_batch_sizes_unified`: Verifies calculation logic across fractional batch sizes, gradient accumulation steps, and expansion factors.
  - `test_fractional_per_device_batch_size_calculations`: Verifies config initialization with fractional train and eval batch sizes.
- `tests/unit/gradient_accumulation_nnx_test.py`:
  - `test_fractional_per_device_batch_size_accumulates_all_samples`: Verifies gradient accumulation across all 4 samples without data dropping when `per_device_batch_size = 0.25`.
  - `test_fractional_eval_microbatch_reshaping_and_accumulation`: Verifies microbatch reshaping and metric accumulation for eval without data dropping.

Commands to run the tests:
```bash
pytest tests/unit/pyconfig_test.py -k "calculate_global_batch_sizes_unified or fractional_per_device_batch_size"
pytest tests/unit/gradient_accumulation_nnx_test.py -k "fractional"
